source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: mechanism-level review
finding: Maps ten historical architectures (ACT-R, Soar, CLARION, LIDA, Hearsay-II, BDI, MIDCA, ICARUS, EPIC, Sigma) onto 8 agent runtimes and 42 mechanism systems. Codes evidence relation E1-E4 and migration depth D0-D4 separately.
numbers: 10 architectures, 8 runtime families, 42 mechanism records; corpus frozen 26 Jul 2026; 6 candidate gaps, 1 closed (GraSP), 5 remain
quote: Modern agents have operationalized substantial parts of adaptive memory, failure recovery
limits: Bounded mapping, no pooled effects. Second-author recoding of D3/D4 claims not yet done. No experiment tests the five residual bundles. Search recall not estimated.
agent_relevance: Best single design check for our schema: most Soar/ACT-R parts exist in agents already, but as separate pieces, not coupled.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: mechanism-level review - ACT-R mapping
finding: ACT-R couples three things: what enters working state, how long retrieval takes, and which action is worth doing (learned utility). Agent memory systems (AgeMem, Memory-R1, MemCon, DeltaMem, A-MAC) learn memory operations as policy actions; the review codes this E3/D4 but as a partial match.
numbers: Memory systems coded E3/D4; ACT-R activation and production utility are two coupled but distinct subsystems
limits: Agent systems train a policy; ACT-R has an accessibility law (frequency, recency, context). Latency is rarely used as an action cost. Residual bundle: activation with latency and action utility.
agent_relevance: Ranking memory by recency, use count and context is cheap; using retrieval cost in action choice is the unexplored part. Keep it small.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: mechanism-level review - Soar mapping
finding: Soar chain is typed failure -> scoped child substate -> typed result returned -> chunking into a future rule. Agent systems cover pieces: PALADIN and AgentDebugX classify tool errors; Shepherd gives reversible branches; Reflexion and AgentHER learn from failures.
numbers: PALADIN/AgentDebugX E3/D3; Shepherd E2/D3; Reflexion/AgentHER E3/D4; residual bundle B2 (typed impasse + isolated substate + resolution compilation) still open
quote: Retry or reflection captures only a fragment when it lacks the typed parent-child state and compilation edge.
limits: Openness claim is limited to the bounded search.
agent_relevance: Supports our impasse operator idea: the unique Soar part is typed impasse plus returned result plus compilation, not reflection alone.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: mechanism-level review - residual bundles
finding: Five untested residual bundles: activation with latency and utility; typed impasse with substates and compilation; bounded content competition with broadcast; persistent intention with reconsideration; uncertainty with resource allocation and stopping. Skill-governance bundle closed because GraSP already does calibrated multi-skill selection, typed compilation, verification, bounded repair and replanning.
numbers: 5 residual bundles; 1 closed; GraSP coded E3/D4
limits: Authors run no experiment on the bundles. These are hypotheses, not results.
agent_relevance: Ready list of what is not yet in the field; each is a testable ablation for our scaffold.

source: Fan & Lan (2026) From Cognitive Architectures to Language Agents: mechanism-level review - validity limits
finding: Authors list what is missing: no independent second-author codes, no comparison of residual bundles against D3/D4 baselines, no search-recall estimate. Mapping makes no performance claim for historical mechanisms.
numbers: 0 independent coders; 0 experiments on the 5 bundles
limits: Single review, July 2026, from a company authors group; D-codes are subjective.
agent_relevance: Treat its depth codes as a map, not as proof that a mechanism helps.

source: Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan, Griffiths (2023) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Frames agents as working memory plus long-term memory (episodic, semantic, procedural), an action space split into internal (reason, retrieve, learn) and external, and a decision loop. Uses Soar as the model case and files Reflexion, Voyager, Generative Agents and ReAct inside it.
numbers: Conceptual paper, no new benchmark numbers
quote: we propose a blueprint to structure such agents.
limits: Authors call it a blueprint; not an evaluated system. Soar impasse subgoaling is described but largely left open for LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Standard vocabulary for mapping; our states and operators can be checked against its memory and action split.

source: Kirk, Wray, Laird (2023) Exploiting Language Models as a Source of Knowledge for Cognitive Agents
finding: Soar group position paper: use LLMs as an external task-knowledge source and let the cognitive architecture raise precision. Describes three integration patterns with costs and benefits.
numbers: 3 integration patterns; no benchmark table
quote: cognitive capabilities... can be applied to the LLM to improve the precision and correctness of the task knowledge
limits: Conceptual; says LLM knowledge production is unreliable.
agent_relevance: Division of labour: LLM gives broad associative proposals, the scaffold checks and stores curated knowledge. Matches our guardrail approach.

source: Wu, Oltramari, Francis, Giles, Ritter (2024) Cognitive LLMs: LLM-ACTR
finding: Injects ACT-R model decision traces into the last hidden layers of a LLaMA model plus a classification head, then fine-tunes. Tested on a Design for Manufacturing choice task.
numbers: Hold-out accuracy 0.6576 / NLL 0.6534 vs plain LLaMA 0.3564 / 1.1330; chance 0.4826 / 0.6931
limits: Small task; needs fine-tuning, not a prompt scaffold; abstract claims advantage over chain-of-thought baselines but the table compares to LLaMA.
agent_relevance: Shows ACT-R knowledge can help a model only through weight training; weak evidence for a prompt-only scaffold.

source: Wu et al. (2024) LLM-ACTR - limits
finding: Complex decisions are captured worse: multi-facet targets (choice plus strategy) drop accuracy. Concatenating ACT-R embeddings with LLM embeddings gave no significant gain over LLM embeddings alone in an extra test.
numbers: Single facet accuracy 0.64, NLL 0.63 (10 folds); multi facet accuracy 0.42, NLL 1.18; concatenation test accuracy 0.71 for both
limits: Authors' own appendix; ragged tensors from variable trace lengths block the fuller embedding.
agent_relevance: Negative boundary: a partial transfer of architecture trace into an LLM loses detail.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: natural language to generative symbolic rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: LLM generates Soar rules from natural language, with Soar execution feedback in a generator-critic loop and a retrieved case base. Tested on 5 task groups, Gemini-2.5 and Qwen-max.
numbers: Success rate 86% (Gemini-2.5-flash) and 91% (Qwen-max) vs one-shot 55% and 66%; zero-shot 0%; manual rules 84%. Hard-case gain +56.67 points (Gemini)
limits: Small set of Soar tasks; authors note prior LLM-Soar work lacked experimental validation.
agent_relevance: Execution feedback from a symbolic architecture and a case memory help an LLM write correct rules.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym - ablation and scale inversion
finding: Removing the critic hurt most; the smaller Flash model with the framework beat the larger Pro model with one-shot prompting.
numbers: Remove critic: SR -23% overall, -37% on hard cases, decision cycles above 1000x minimum; remove basic knowledge base -17%; remove case base -14%; Flash with framework 86% vs Pro one-shot 55%
limits: Same small task set; ablation is of a pipeline, not of an architecture part.
agent_relevance: Feedback loop is worth more than extra knowledge; structure can beat model size.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Agent stores verbal self-reflections in episodic memory after failed trials; mapped to chunking-like learning by the 2026 review (E3/D4).
numbers: HumanEval Python pass@1 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1; AlfWorld +22 points absolute in 12 steps; HotPotQA +20 points; MBPP Python 77.1 vs 80.1 (below baseline)
limits: Needs unit tests or environment signal. MBPP false-positive test rate 16.3% vs 1.4% on HumanEval explains the weaker gain.
agent_relevance: Learning from failure works when there is an external signal; keep a verifier.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion - ablation
finding: Without self-generated unit tests, reflection harms: agent cannot tell if the current code is right.
numbers: HumanEval Rust hardest 50: no test generation 52% vs baseline 60% vs full 68%
limits: Subset of 50 hard problems; one model (GPT-4).
agent_relevance: Supports guardrail: no reflection step without a check.

source: Huang et al. (2023/2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Re-tests self-correction without oracle labels. Without ground truth, accuracy falls or stays flat; earlier gains came from oracle labels deciding when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 after one round; GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7 after two rounds; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0 after five calls; HotpotQA 49 -> 43
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
limits: Prompts taken from source papers; newer models or trained verifiers may differ.
agent_relevance: Direct failed-replication evidence: reflection alone is not a Soar-style resolution.

source: Huang et al. (2024) - oracle-label contrast
finding: With oracle labels the same loop looks strong, which shows the gain is from the label.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 95.5 (oracle); HotpotQA 26.0 -> 49.0; GPT-4 HotpotQA 29.0 -> 59.0 (oracle); GSM8K: 74.7% of GPT-3.5 answers unchanged
limits: Oracle is unavailable in real use.
agent_relevance: Any impasse-detection should use outside evidence, not self-judgment.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: Minecraft agent with automatic curriculum, a skill library of verified code (compare ICARUS / chunking-like reuse), and iterative prompting with self-verification.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x more than baselines; wooden tool 15.3x faster, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only agent reaching diamond; map 2.3x longer
limits: 3 runs per method; GPT-4 needed.
agent_relevance: Compiled, verified skills reused later is the agent version of production learning.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager - ablations
finding: Each part matters; curriculum and self-verification matter most; skill library plateaus without growth.
numbers: Random curriculum: -93% items; remove self-verification: -73%; without skill library plateaus late
limits: Single environment (Minecraft).
agent_relevance: Verifier and goal ordering are the load-bearing parts, not only memory.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Induces reusable workflows from successful trajectories into memory (procedural learning), online and offline.
numbers: WebArena +12.0 points, +51.1% relative success over BrowserGym baseline; +7.6% relative over SteP with human workflows; Mind2Web cross-task +24.6% relative step success
limits: Gains shrink when tasks differ from learned workflows; agents resist newly added actions.
agent_relevance: Learned routines from successes beat hand-written ones in this test.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents
finding: Memory stream retrieved by recency, importance and relevance, plus reflection and planning; ablated each part.
numbers: TrueSkill mu: full 29.89, no reflection or planning 25.64, crowdworkers 22.95, no memory/plan/reflection 21.21; d=8.16 full vs prior work; Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001; 100 evaluators
limits: Rated believability, not task success; agents embellish memories.
agent_relevance: Activation-like retrieval scoring plus reflection raised believability.

source: Packer et al. (2023) MemGPT
finding: Operating-system style paging of main context and archival storage managed by the model through function calls.
numbers: Deep memory retrieval accuracy: GPT-3.5 38.7% -> 66.9%; GPT-4 32.1% -> 92.5%; GPT-4 Turbo 35.3% -> 93.4%
limits: Authors built the DMR task themselves.
agent_relevance: Explicit working versus long-term memory management gave large gains.

source: Yan et al. (2026) Memory-R1
finding: RL-trained memory manager (ADD, UPDATE, DELETE, NOOP) plus answer agent; closest to learned ACT-R-style memory control in the review.
numbers: 152 training QA pairs; LLaMA-3.1-8B: +28% F1, +34% BLEU-1, +30% judge vs Mem0; Qwen-2.5-7B: beats MemoryOS by 24.5% F1
limits: Needs RL training; LoCoMo mainly.
agent_relevance: Outcome-driven memory operations help; not a prompt-only result.

source: Hu, Lu, Clune (2025) Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS)
finding: Meta agent writes code for new agent designs from an archive; review maps this to MIDCA meta-control at design time.
numbers: DROP F1 +13.6; MGSM +14.4%; transfer GSM8K +25.9%, GSM-Hard +13.2% over hand-designed baselines
limits: Design time only; costly search.
agent_relevance: Searching scaffold structure can work, but our schema is fixed deliberately.

source: Laird, Lebiere, Rosenbloom, Stocco (2025) Extend the Common Model of Cognition with Metacognition
finding: Notes substate mechanisms exist in Soar and Sigma but not ACT-R; proposes metacognition as reasoning over explicit representations of the agent's own cognition.
numbers: Conceptual
limits: Proposal only.
agent_relevance: Impasse subgoaling is Soar-specific; relevant to our impasse operator.

source: Always-On Agents survey (2026)
finding: Survey on persistent state; a search snippet says it links the ACT-R lineage to LLM agents through CoALA memory modules.
numbers: Not extracted
limits: Seen only in search results.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Joshi & Ustun (2024) Comparing LLMs for Prompt-Enhanced ACT-R and Soar Model Development
finding: AAAI symposium paper comparing ChatGPT-4 and Bard for writing ACT-R and Soar models.
numbers: Not extracted
limits: Seen only in search listing.
agent_relevance: Not opened; follow-up.
